stem: A tokenizer maps words to integer IDs. Which data structure best represents this mapping?

options.text: A list — because you can loop through words
A dictionary — maps each word (key) to its ID (value)
A boolean — either the word exists or it doesn't
An integer — IDs are just numbers

explanation_after: Tokenizer vocabulary = {'hello': 7592, 'world': 995, ...}. A dictionary is perfect: O(1) lookup. The GPT-2 tokenizer has 50,257 tokens.

stem: How does a Python dictionary organise its entries?
explanation_after: Every dictionary entry has a key (what you look up by) and a value (what you get back). Keys must be unique.

.get(key, default) returns the default value when the key is missing instead of raising KeyError. Since 'batch_size' isn't in config, it returns 32. This is safer than config['batch_size'] whenever a key might be optional, like reading hyperparameters that have sensible defaults.

.items() yields (key, value) tuples, and unpacking them into name, score gives each pair directly, so print(name, score) prints them space-separated. Dictionaries preserve insertion order since Python 3.7, so 'Alice' prints before 'Bob'.

stem: A bag-of-words model counts word frequency in a document using a dictionary called counts. Which line correctly increments the count for a word that may or may not already be a key?
explanation_after: If word isn't already a key, counts[word] += 1 raises a KeyError because it tries to read counts[word] before it exists. counts.get(word, 0) safely returns 0 for a first-time word, so adding 1 correctly starts the count at 1. This counting dictionary is the first step in building a bag-of-words feature vector — once the vocabulary is fixed in order, the dictionary's values become the numbers in an ML input vector.
